title: The Quantum Mechanics of Rare Events: From Quantum Walks to Stochastic Inflation
authors: Daniel Green, Kshitij Gupta, Akhil Premkumar
abstract: Rare fluctuations in physical systems depend on the detailed microphysics responsible for the fluctuations. In classical statistical systems, the large deviation principle has elucidated the role of semi-classics in describing this regime, and has simultaneously provided a the mathematical foundation of statistical mechanics. Large deviation theory for quantum system is considerably less developed. As all physical systems are fundamentally quantum mechanical, this leaves a major gap in our understanding of rare fluctuations relevant to statistical physics, cosmology, and more. In this paper, we develop the practical aspects of the theory of large deviations relevant for calculating rare events in physical systems from quantum walks to cosmology. We first analyze the case of the anharmonic oscillator coupled to a bath, showing explicitly how the system evolves from dominantly statistical (e.g. thermal) to quantum fluctuations. We then generalize these results, showing that the dominant rare fluctuations minimize the measurement-induced relative entropy. This perspective provides a thermodynamic description of a wide range of open quantum systems. We apply these results to random walks that arise in cosmology through stochastic inflation. We show that the evolution of the density matrix of long wavelength fields on a fixed de Sitter background breaks the KMS symmetry, giving rise to a stationary density matrix that does not respect detailed balance.
summary: This paper develops the theory of large deviations for quantum systems, which is crucial for understanding rare events in physics. It demonstrates that these fluctuations can be characterized by minimizing measurement-induced relative entropy across various models. The work applies this framework successfully to both condensed matter analogs (anharmonic oscillators) and fundamental cosmology problems like stochastic inflation.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a practical theory of large deviations for quantum systems, addressing a major gap in understanding rare fluctuations relevant to statistical physics and cosmology.
main_result: The paper shows that dominant rare quantum fluctuations minimize the measurement-induced relative entropy, providing a thermodynamic description applicable from quantum walks to cosmological field evolution.
method: The authors analyze open quantum systems using techniques involving quantum fidelity maximization and minimizing measurement-induced relative entropy, extending classical large deviation principles.
model_or_system: Models include the anharmonic oscillator coupled to a bath, general quantum random walks, and long wavelength scalar fields evolving on a fixed de Sitter background in cosmology.
key_observables: Measurement-induced relative entropy, Quantum Fidelity ($\mathcal{F}$), rate function $I(\alpha)$, and the breakdown of KMS symmetry.
important_parameters: Temperature (thermal vs. quantum regimes), coupling constants ($\lambda$), and cosmological scale factors defining de Sitter space.
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes Gaussian noise for deriving diffusion equations, and it builds upon established large deviation theory from classical statistical mechanics.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the crossover between classical random (thermal), quantum mechanical (WKB), and numerical instanton contributions to the probability distribution $P(x)$ at large distances.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first analyzing the anharmonic oscillator's transition from thermal to quantum behavior, then generalizing this using relative entropy minimization for abstract quantum walks, and finally applying these concepts to random walks arising in stochastic inflation/de Sitter cosmology.
why_interesting: It bridges foundational statistical mechanics (large deviations) with modern open quantum systems dynamics and high-energy astrophysics (cosmology), providing tools applicable to non-equilibrium quantum processes.

Figure 4: A three-site lattice sustaining a nonequilibrium steady state (NESS). (Left) Individual transition rates to/from each site. Each bond has a dominant (thick) and a reverse (thin, gray) rate, with πapab ̸= πbpba and cyclically for (b, c) and (c, a). (Right) The resulting net circulation. Since πa, πb, πc are constant in time, this current is stationary: mass leaving a is exactly replen- ished via c →a, with no accumulation anywhere. This persistent circulation, despite a perfectly stationary density, is the source of housekeeping entropy production.
